doc.title: Curtis Fuller — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Janice Robinson on the road and Melba Liston
summary: Fuller recounts rooming arrangements with trombonist Janice Robinson and Melba Liston's presence in Quincy Jones's band.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: That isn't it is very important to Dr. Taylor, is the cultivation, or the equalization of the participation of women in this music. But, does that hearken back to may be the experience of Melba Liston and how important she was? Talk about that relationship
Oh yeah, that was a beautiful relationship. I've seen her sit on the bandstand and cry. And that organization actually had to women and it. Patty Bowen was on piano.

Yeah, Quincy. Melba was also in Dizzy’s bandwidth me. There was one band that I was, Chuck Israel Orchestra with a bunch of people. Janice Robinson was fresh out of Eastman. She was a good little girl and I was her hero. Actually, both of us being black, the pitted us together with both of us in a room on the road. I actually sat in the lobby so she could have the room and be a little lady, you know? We talked together the other day and they laughed. “Is that what you were doing? Is that why you were gone?” “Yep, I was giving you your space.”
So, they actually, rather than having you room with another male, they put you with a woman.

Well, because we were the same cloth, the same patchwork. We were just talking about that with Janice. She was thanking me for, you know, giving her that respect. But, I didn’t have to take it to that dimension. She thought I was just hanging out. But, I was close by. Dennis was a young girl and I just wanted her to have a you know… She was conscious of it. Because even when she got in bases band she worked too many clothes. She was covering up a lovely body and stuff, just so guys wouldn't hit on her. She looked like a little old maiden. You don't have to go

that extreme. Guys are going to be guys and you'll learn to get through that. You know the girls and the basketball team, you're going to get those whistles and it is demeaning sometimes. Her father was a preacher and stuff and I tried to give her the encouragement that, "you are here to play and that is the essence of what you're here for."
